title: Namdev's kite string
hook: a song from a Marathi tailor turns up in Punjab, and a boy keeps his eye on a kite string
carry: simran: the mind on god, like a kite string

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poet-sadhus. Kirtan: singing God's form keeps him near. Gujarat ends here, and Punjab begins.

A boy on a rooftop is flying a paper kite. His friends are around him, laughing, teasing, talking over each other, and he's laughing with them. But watch his hands, his eyes. Whatever he's saying, part of him never leaves the string. That picture comes from a song by Namdev, the tailor-saint of Maharashtra this path met last year, singing to Vitthal. And the song is kept far to the north, in Punjab, in a book Sikhs honor as their living Guru. Today, Punjab, where devotional songs from many places ended up living side by side.
screen: `A BOY AND A KITE.` → `A SONG FROM MAHARASHTRA.` → `KEPT IN PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: Punjab is a crossroads, and the songs show it. First, the book. The Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs revere as their Guru, holds the hymns of the Sikh Gurus, and also songs by bhagats, devotees from outside that line: Namdev from Maharashtra, Kabir the weaver of Kashi, Ravidas, and Sheikh Farid, a Sufi of Punjab, among others. Sikhs sing them in the gurdwara beside the Gurus' own hymns. Hindus honor Namdev, Kabir and Ravidas in their own traditions too. So here is ground both share, each standing on it in its own way. Then, Namdev himself. Tradition says that late in life he traveled north and lived in Punjab, and a village there, Ghuman, remembers him with a shrine. A tailor from the Marathi country, honored in a Punjabi village. And now the kite. In paraphrase, the hymn gives a string of pictures. A boy flies his kite and talks with his friends, but his mind stays on the string. Young women carry water pots on their heads, laughing and chatting as they walk, but their attention stays on the pot. A cow grazes far out in the fields, her mind on her calf. A mother goes about her work, her heart on the child in the cradle. That, the song says, is how the mind can stay on God: not by stopping life, but in the middle of it. Hindus call this smarana, remembering God; Sikhs call it simran, keeping the Name in mind. Two traditions, one practice, kept in one song. The talk goes on. Underneath, one thread holds.
screen: `PUNJAB, A CROSSROADS OF SONG` · `SAINTS FROM MANY PLACES IN ONE BOOK` · `NAMDEV REMEMBERED IN A PUNJAB VILLAGE` · `THE MIND ON THE STRING` · `SMARANA · SIMRAN`

segments.voice: Let sounds come and go around you, the way friends chatter around the boy on the roof, and keep one light thread of attention on a name, the way his fingers stay on the string. If you pray, let it be a name of God you love: Vitthal, as Namdev sang, or Waheguru, as Sikhs say; if you don't, let the thread be your breath. When you notice you've let go, pick the string back up.
Punjab's shared devotional ground. Today, Namdev's kite song: simran, the mind on God in the middle of life. Today's word.
Your line: simran, the mind on God, like a kite string. A tailor's song, sung in a Sikh scripture far from home. Same time tomorrow.
